One-page synthesis

Core thesis: In adult solid organ transplant recipients at least 1 year after transplant, a second high-dose influenza vaccine given 4–6 weeks after an initial high-dose dose did not significantly improve the prespecified baseline-to-4-month immunogenicity endpoint, but exploratory post-randomization analyses suggest the booster may better maintain binding antibody responses later in the season.

The trial randomized 65 participants after all had received one high-dose Fluzone dose: 32 received a second high-dose vaccine and 33 received placebo. The study was designed for 47 participants per arm but did not reach its enrollment target. The primary immunogenicity analysis used geometric mean fold rise (GMFR) in ID80 neutralizing and binding antibody titers from baseline to 4 months, with generalized estimating equations, robust variance, multiple imputation for missing 4-month titers, and Holm correction across strain/assay comparisons.

Across all strains and both primary assay types, baseline-to-4-month GMFRs numerically favored the 2-dose arm, but no between-group comparison was statistically significant. In the exploratory 1-month-to-4-month interval, binding titers were better maintained in the 2-dose arm: adjusted differences remained significant for Austria (GMR 1.30, adjusted p=0.008), Darwin (1.38, adjusted p=0.008), and Phuket (1.36, adjusted p=0.012), while Wisconsin did not remain significant after correction. No ID80 neutralization comparison remained significant after Holm adjustment.

Clinical outcomes were too sparse for effectiveness conclusions. Two laboratory-confirmed influenza cases occurred, both in the 1-dose group, but only 6 of 16 participants reporting influenza-like illness underwent respiratory viral testing. Safety signals were not increased with the booster: any adverse event occurred in 69% vs 67%, and solicited reactogenicity was grade 1. However, the sample was far too small to establish uncommon safety outcomes.

Main interpretive constraint: The paper's most favorable statistically significant findings come from exploratory post-randomization analyses, whereas the prespecified primary immunogenicity analysis was negative. The trial is therefore hypothesis-supporting rather than practice-changing.

Clinical question / PICO

Population

Adults ≥18 years, ≥1 year after kidney, liver, heart, lung, or pancreas transplant. Key exclusions included pregnancy, lymphocyte-depleting or B-cell-directed therapy within 3 months, prednisone ≥20 mg/day, prior influenza vaccination during the enrollment season, and severe influenza-vaccine allergy.

Intervention

High-dose Fluzone at baseline plus a second high-dose Fluzone dose 4–6 weeks later.

Comparator

High-dose Fluzone at baseline plus saline placebo 4–6 weeks later.

Outcomes

Primary: baseline-to-4-month fold change in geometric mean ID80 neutralizing and binding antibody titers. Secondary: influenza-related clinical events and safety. Prespecified exploratory analyses examined ID50 and interval-specific GMFRs.

Section condensation

Introduction / rationale

Solid organ transplant recipients have higher risk of severe influenza and often generate weaker responses to standard-dose influenza vaccines. Prior work suggests that increasing antigen dose or using booster strategies can improve immunogenicity, but randomized evidence directly comparing one versus two high-dose doses within the same influenza season in adult SOT recipients was lacking.

The study therefore tested whether a two-dose high-dose regimen would produce stronger and more durable influenza-specific antibody responses than a single high-dose dose.

Methods — design, intervention, and follow-up

This was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, single-center trial across the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 seasons. All participants received high-dose Fluzone at baseline; 4–6 weeks later, 65 participants were randomized 1:1 by the investigational pharmacy using permuted blocks to receive either a second high-dose dose or saline placebo. Participants and clinical/research personnel remained blinded until study completion. The final visit occurred 16–18 weeks after baseline.

Fluzone HD contained 60 μg hemagglutinin per strain. The 2023–2024 vaccine was quadrivalent and the 2024–2025 vaccine trivalent. The study's antibody assays used Austria (B/Victoria), Darwin (H3N2), Phuket (B/Yamagata), and Wisconsin (H1N1) cell-based strains with reported 98–100% amino-acid homology to the vaccine's egg-based HA components.

Methods — laboratory and statistics

Neutralization used replication-restricted influenza reporter viruses, with ID50 and ID80 estimated from logistic curves. Binding antibodies were measured by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay and reported in arbitrary units/mL. Samples with >30% replicate coefficient of variation were repeated.

The planned sample was 47 per arm for 80% power to detect a between-group geometric mean ratio of 3.0, but enrollment fell short. Analyses were intention-to-treat. GMRs were estimated with generalized estimating equations on log-transformed titers using robust variance. Multiple imputation addressed missing 4-month titers; complete-case analyses were also performed. Holm correction controlled family-wise error across strains/assays. Phuket analyses were limited to the 2023–2024 season.

Results — enrollment and baseline characteristics

Of 228 prescreened individuals, 74 enrolled, 67 received the first high-dose vaccine, and 65 were randomized: 32 to a second high-dose dose and 33 to placebo. Complete serologic data at all 3 visits were available for 27 and 31 participants, respectively. Baseline characteristics were generally similar, although the small sample produced visible imbalances in sex and transplant type.

The median age was 61 years overall; 67.7% were male and 92.3% were White. Kidney was the most recent transplant in 50.8% and liver in 24.6%; 64.6% were >5 years from their most recent transplant. Tacrolimus and mycophenolate were each used in 67.7%, prednisone in 41.5%, and 86.2% had received seasonal influenza vaccine in the prior season.

Results — immunogenicity

After the first baseline high-dose vaccine, ID80 neutralizing and binding GMFRs exceeded 1.0 for all strains at 1 month. In the primary baseline-to-4-month analysis, every GMFR comparison numerically favored two doses, but none reached statistical significance after adjustment. The largest primary numerical difference was for Phuket binding antibody (GMR 1.30, 95% CI 0.99–1.71; unadjusted p=0.057; adjusted p=0.456).

In the exploratory 1-month-to-4-month interval, the 1-dose arm generally showed declining titers while the 2-dose arm remained near or above its 1-month level. Binding responses significantly favored the second dose for Austria, Darwin, and Phuket after Holm correction; Wisconsin did not. Neutralizing ID80 differences did not remain significant after correction, and ID50 analyses likewise did not show statistically significant between-group differences.

Results — clinical outcomes and safety

One participant in the 2-dose group died of influenza-unrelated causes, leaving 64 for clinical outcome analysis. Sixteen participants reported influenza-like illness (7 vs 9); only 6 were tested. Two laboratory-confirmed influenza infections occurred, both in the 1-dose group, 5–6 months after baseline. There were no influenza-related hospitalizations, ICU admissions, ventilatory support events, or deaths.

Any clinical adverse event occurred in 22/32 (69%) versus 22/33 (67%). Nearly all recorded events were grade 1–2. Solicited reactogenicity within 7 days occurred in 19/65 (29%) and was entirely grade 1. The apparent 19% vs 39% group difference was driven largely by reactogenicity after the first dose, before the randomized second injection; reactogenicity after the second study injection was similar between vaccine and placebo. One grade 3 liver rejection occurred in the 1-dose arm and one death from subarachnoid hemorrhage with acute myeloid leukemia occurred in the 2-dose arm; the death was deemed unrelated to study injections.

Discussion, limitations, and conclusion

The authors interpret the exploratory post-randomization findings as evidence that an in-season high-dose booster may enhance or maintain influenza-specific antibody responses in immunosuppressed SOT recipients. They appropriately acknowledge that the primary analysis was not statistically significant and that larger adequately powered studies are needed before inferring clinical benefit.

Major limitations include underenrollment, missing final titers, a single-center cohort dominated by kidney/liver recipients, exclusion of patients <1 year post-transplant, lack of a dedicated peak post-booster visit, end-of-season symptom ascertainment without active surveillance, incomplete respiratory testing, absence of hemagglutination-inhibition correlates, vaccine formulation changes between seasons, and use of highly homologous but not perfectly matched cell-based assay strains. These limitations restrict both causal precision and practice generalizability.

Research transparency

The manuscript reports IRB approval and informed consent; the protocol was considered exempt from an FDA IND under 21 CFR 312.2(b). Data are available from investigators on reasonable request. The authors report no competing interests, and internal University of Minnesota plus NIH intramural support is disclosed.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Read soon. The study is a useful first randomized signal for in-season high-dose influenza boosting in adult SOT recipients, but the negative primary analysis, small underpowered sample, surrogate endpoints, and sparse clinical outcome ascertainment prevent routine-practice conclusions.
Relevance
9/10

Directly addresses vaccination in immunosuppressed transplant recipients and a clinically plausible strategy for improving weak vaccine response.

Evidence basis: randomized transplant-specific clinical trial. Limiting factor: immunogenicity rather than clinical effectiveness. Would rise: clinical outcome data in a larger multicenter cohort.

Novelty
8/10

The authors report this as the first randomized comparison of two versus one high-dose influenza doses within a season in SOT recipients.

Evidence basis: direct study question not previously tested in this population. Limiting factor: concept extends prior booster/high-dose work. Would rise: demonstration of durable clinical protection.

Method strength
7/10

Randomization, placebo control, blinding, prespecified endpoints, multiple-imputation sensitivity, complete-case checks, and multiplicity correction are strengths.

Limiting factor: underenrollment, missing final titers, one center, small arms, no peak post-booster visit. Would rise: target enrollment met, multicenter replication, prespecified post-booster endpoint.

Evidence strength
5/10

The primary comparison is directionally favorable but statistically negative; the strongest positive findings are exploratory binding-antibody outcomes.

Evidence basis: adjusted GMRs and CIs from Table 2/3. Limiting factor: surrogate immunogenicity, underpowering, exploratory inference. Would rise: replicated primary endpoint and clinically meaningful outcomes.

External validity
5/10

Participants were mostly White, kidney/liver transplant recipients, generally years after transplant, and recruited at a single center.

Limiting factor: little evidence for early post-transplant, lung transplant, more heavily immunosuppressed, or diverse populations. Would rise: multicenter enrollment with transplant-type and immunosuppression strata.

Implementation value
5/10

The regimen is simple and operationally feasible, but the paper does not establish that a routine booster changes patient-centered outcomes or should be adopted.

Limiting factor: no clinical effectiveness endpoint and no health-system implementation analysis. Would rise: effectiveness, cost/logistics, timing, and guideline integration data.

Strengths

  • Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design with blinded second-injection allocation.
  • Clear immunologic assay methods and longitudinal sampling across an influenza season.
  • Multiple imputation plus complete-case analyses and Holm multiplicity correction.
  • Clinically relevant immunocompromised population.
  • Transparent acknowledgment that enrollment shortfall reduced power.

Critical limitations

  • Primary endpoint not statistically significant. The most persuasive positive results are exploratory.
  • Underpowered. Planned 47 per arm; randomized 32 and 33.
  • Surrogate outcomes. Binding/neutralizing antibody responses are biologically informative but do not establish reduced influenza morbidity.
  • Clinical surveillance was weak. Only 6 of 16 participants with ILI were tested, and ILI was collected at season end.
  • No peak post-booster visit. The design cannot directly quantify peak response 4–6 weeks after the second dose.
  • Restricted generalizability. Mostly kidney/liver recipients; >1 year post-SOT; few lung recipients; single center; predominantly White cohort.
  • Assay/vaccine complexity. Vaccine formulation changed between seasons, Phuket was season-restricted, and assay strains were highly homologous but not exact vaccine matches.
  • Supplement not available for this review. Supplementary sensitivity analyses and detailed AE tables could not be independently appraised.

Practice translation

Use now? No—not as a routine booster policy on this trial alone. The study supports biological plausibility and justifies further study, but it does not establish clinical effectiveness, a patient-centered benefit, or a sufficiently certain primary immunogenicity benefit.

What the evidence can support

  • A second high-dose influenza dose 4–6 weeks later appears immunologically active and did not show an obvious increase in common adverse events in this small trial.
  • The booster may help maintain binding-antibody titers later in the season.
  • Larger multicenter trials are justified.

What the evidence cannot support

  • Routine two-dose high-dose vaccination for all adult SOT recipients.
  • Reduction in influenza infection, hospitalization, ICU admission, or mortality.
  • Safety conclusions for uncommon events.
  • Generalization to <1 year post-transplant or substantially more immunosuppressed recipients.
  • A specific practice recommendation independent of current guidelines and local transplant policy.

Implementation / research takeaways

Best use

Background evidence for transplant-vaccine strategy discussions, protocol-development hypotheses, and justification for a definitive multicenter booster trial.

Do not use for

Standalone justification for changing seasonal influenza vaccination schedules in SOT recipients.

Next study design

Multicenter, adequately powered trial stratified by transplant type/time since transplant and immunosuppression, with a dedicated post-booster peak visit, active respiratory surveillance, standardized testing, HAI plus neutralization/binding assays, and patient-centered clinical outcomes.

High-value mechanistic question

Does the second high-dose dose truly raise peak immunity, or mainly slow seasonal antibody decline? The current interval analysis is more consistent with maintenance than a large secondary rise.
